passage.quote:
Scientific-computing examples exercise the same tensor and numerical interfaces
outside neural networks. The quadrilateral Poisson example constructs and solves
a finite-element discretization of a boundary-value problem. Its Lean/TorchLean
reference and binary64 PTX execution distinguish numerical comparisons from
formal solver, kernel-correspondence and continuous-equation guarantees.

summary: Solve the unit-square Q1–Q4 Poisson discretization using shared nodes, tensor contractions and an interior-only iterative solve.
Require fresh residual checks for convergence and expose numerical failures and iteration limits.
Distinguish executable binary64 results, exact residual certificates, empirical Python comparisons and unproved continuous PDE or PTX instruction claims.
Provide a separate PTX execution responsibility while retaining explicit proof and hardware boundaries.

from.quote:
The mesh uses Gauss–Lobatto interpolation nodes, including both cell endpoints.
Adjacent cells share endpoint nodes. Gauss–Legendre quadrature approximates an
integral by a weighted sum of values at selected points. One-dimensional basis
values and derivatives are reused in each coordinate. The operator acts through
successive small TorchLean matrix products instead of constructing the full
global stiffness matrix. Contributions at shared nodes are added, and solving
uses only interior unknowns; boundary entries are extended by exact zeros.

passage.quote:
/-- Two one-coordinate contractions per gradient, followed by their transposes.
The same definition can be instantiated with Float or with exact real numbers. -/
def localAction [Storage α] [Add α] [Mul α] [Zero α]
    (b d : Mat α q m) (w : Mat α q q) (u : Mat α m m) : Mat α m m :=
  let dx := Spec.matMulSpec (Spec.matMulSpec b u) (transpose d)
  let dy := Spec.matMulSpec (Spec.matMulSpec d u) (transpose b)
  plus (Spec.matMulSpec (Spec.matMulSpec (transpose b) (hadamard w dx)) d)
       (Spec.matMulSpec (Spec.matMulSpec (transpose d) (hadamard w dy)) b)

from.quote:
The linear solver is Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradients: it uses the
operator's diagonal to rescale the iterative updates. It returns convergence,
breakdown or iteration-limit status. Success requires a newly computed residual
(the load minus the operator applied to the candidate solution) within the
requested tolerance. A small recursive residual alone cannot certify success;
false recursive convergence restarts from the measured residual. All loops have
explicit finite limits, and invalid mesh sizes, degrees, tolerances, vectors and
quadrature setup are rejected.

passage.quote:
/-- Bounded PCG, including frozen steps, true-residual checks and restart.
Success is a measured residual criterion, not a PDE-error certificate. -/
def solvePCG (o : Operator) (rhsFull : Array Float) (opts : Options := {}) : Except String Result := do
  checkVector rhsFull o.mesh.points.size
  if !opts.rtol.isFinite || !opts.atol.isFinite || opts.rtol < 0 || opts.atol < 0 ||
      (opts.rtol == 0 && opts.atol == 0) || opts.checkEvery == 0 then throw "invalid solver options"
  let rhs := restrict o rhsFull
  let rhsNorm := norm rhs
  let tolerance := max opts.atol (opts.rtol*rhsNorm)
  let finish := fun x it residual reason =>
    Result.mk (extend o x) reason it residual (if rhsNorm == 0 then 0 else residual/rhsNorm) tolerance
  let mut x := Array.replicate rhs.size 0.0
  if !rhsNorm.isFinite then return finish x 0 rhsNorm .breakdown
  if rhsNorm ≤ tolerance then return finish x 0 rhsNorm .converged
  if opts.maxiter == 0 then return finish x 0 rhsNorm .maxiter
  let diagonal := restrict o o.diagonal
  let precondition := fun r => tab rhs.size fun i => r[i]!/diagonal[i]!
  let mut r := rhs
  let mut z := precondition r
  let mut p := z
  let mut rho := dot r z
  let mut active := true; let mut broken := false
  let mut residualNorm := rhsNorm
  for it in [1:opts.maxiter+1] do
    let ap := applyInteriorRaw o p
    let denominator := dot p ap
    let valid := denominator.isFinite && denominator > 0 && rho.isFinite && rho > 0
    broken := broken || (active && !valid)
    let useStep := active && valid
    let alpha := if useStep then rho/denominator else 0
    x := combine x alpha p
    r := combine r (-alpha) ap
    z := precondition r
    let rhoNext := dot r z
    broken := broken || (active && !rhoNext.isFinite)
    let beta := if useStep then rhoNext/(if rho > 0 then rho else 1) else 0
    p := combine z beta p
    rho := rhoNext
    active := useStep && dot r r > tolerance*tolerance && !broken
    if it % opts.checkEvery == 0 || it == opts.maxiter then
      let trueResidual := combine rhs (-1) (applyInteriorRaw o x)
      residualNorm := norm trueResidual
      if !residualNorm.isFinite then return finish x it residualNorm .breakdown
      if residualNorm ≤ tolerance then return finish x it residualNorm .converged
      if broken then return finish x it residualNorm .breakdown
      if !active then
        r := trueResidual; z := precondition r; p := z; rho := dot r z; active := true
  return finish x opts.maxiter residualNorm .maxiter

from.quote:
The executable reference uses Lean's native Float (binary64) on the CPU.
Its tensor contractions call TorchLean's matrix multiplication specification,
instantiated with Float. The same local algebra can be instantiated with real
numbers; this does not equate rounded execution with exact real arithmetic.
Quadrature setup computes Legendre roots by bounded Newton iteration rather
than reproducing PyTorch's eigensolver. Node, weight, operator and solution
comparisons check this numerical choice independently. No bitwise equality to
PyTorch's backend is promised.

passage.quote:
/-- Setup for the two-to-six-point rules used by Q1–Q4 (also accepts one).
Each root has at most 64 Newton steps and is checked before acceptance. -/
def gaussRule (count : Nat) : Except String (Array Float × Array Float) := do
  if count == 0 || count > 6 then throw "quadrature count must be one through six"
  let mut points := #[]; let mut weights := #[]
  for i in [0:count] do
    let mut z := -(pi*(Float.ofNat i+0.75)/(Float.ofNat count+0.5)).cos
    let mut done := false
    for _ in [0:64] do
      if !done then
        let (v,d) := legendre count z
        let next := z-v/d
        done := (next-z).abs ≤ 1e-15
        z := next
    let (v,d) := legendre count z
    let w := 1/((1-z*z)*d*d)
    if !done || !z.isFinite || !w.isFinite || !(w > 0) || !(z.abs < 1) || v.abs > 2e-14 then
      throw "quadrature root calculation failed"
    points := points.push ((z+1)/2); weights := weights.push w
  return (points,weights)

A sine solution with a known source supplies a reproducible end-to-end example.
Separate quadrature estimates measure errors in the field and its gradient;
these are numerical measurements, not proved bounds on the continuous equation.
The first implementation includes mesh/setup, operator and diagonal, load,
interior restriction, iterative solve and error integration. The reference does not include
differentiation through the solver or binary32 mode,
and it does not establish a convergence theorem, a finite-element error theorem or a verified numerical
relationship to the Python backend. Tests and any Lean theorems state their
own narrower guarantees.
